speaker: Terence Tao
title: Terence Tao: Hardest Problems in Mathematics, Physics & the Future of AI (#472)
question: In mathematics, why can modifying a parameter in a formally verified proof actually be smoother than revising a traditional pen-and-paper proof?
guest: There was a theorem I formalized with a certain constant twelve in the final statement that had to be carried all through the proof, so all the other numbers had to stay consistent with it. A few weeks later, someone improved that twelve to an eleven by reworking some steps. When this happens with pen and paper, every time you change a parameter, you have to check line by line that every single line of your proof still works, because there can be subtle properties of twelve you didn't even realize you were taking advantage of, so a proof can break down in a subtle place. With Lean, you just change twelve to eleven and run the compiler. Out of thousands of lines of code, ninety percent still work, and just a couple are underlined in red. It immediately isolates which steps you need to change, so you can skip over everything that works fine. If you don't hard-code your constants and use smart tactics, you localize the changes to a small area. You make a change, ten things break, you fix those, five break, and the process converges much more smoothly than with pen and paper.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because in a formalized proof, the computer tracks every logical dependency for you. When you change a parameter (say, a constant or exponent) in a proof assistant like Lean, you simply recompile: the system instantly flags exactly which lines break, and everything else is guaranteed to still be correct. You then repair only those specific steps, and once the proof compiles again, you know the whole argument is valid.

With a pen-and-paper proof, the same change forces you to manually re-read the entire argument, checking every place the parameter might matter, including subtle, implicit uses, with a real risk of missing one and introducing an undetected error.

Terence Tao described exactly this when formalizing the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture proof in Lean: when the constant 12 was improved to 11, updating the formal proof took only a short time, since the compiler pinpointed the handful of lines needing fixes. Modular structure helps too: lemmas are stated with precise hypotheses, so changes stay localized, and collaborators can patch separate broken pieces in parallel without needing to trust or recheck each other's work.

Moreover, steps proved by automated tactics—such as linear arithmetic or algebraic solvers—often adapt to updated constants automatically without manual rewriting. Rather than auditing a whole manuscript from scratch, the mathematician only needs to repair the specific proof obligations flagged by the verifier, turning a fragile global rewrite into fast, localized, and reliable maintenance.

noweb.answer:
In a traditional pen-and-paper proof, logical dependencies are woven implicitly into prose, making parameter changes surprisingly fragile. Adjusting a constant, dimension, or bound forces a mathematician to manually re-read the entire argument to check whether hidden assumptions, boundary cases, or delicate inequalities quietly break—a tedious process where subtle errors easily slip through.

By contrast, a formally verified proof behaves like strongly typed software. Because a proof assistant’s kernel tracks every dependency explicitly, changing a parameter triggers an immediate, mechanical audit. Any lemma or step that still compiles is guaranteed to remain valid without human re-inspection, while the system pinpoints the exact lines and subgoals where the new value violates a precondition or breaks an estimate. Moreover, steps driven by automated tactics, such as linear arithmetic solvers or simplifiers, often adapt to the updated parameter automatically. Instead of hunting through pages of dense text for invisible ripple effects, the mathematician receives a precise, exhaustive list of only the steps that genuinely need repair.

A formal proof records all its dependencies explicitly, and its modular lemmas are machine-checked, so revising it becomes a targeted repair job rather than a full re-audit. The verification is also complete and trustworthy. Formalization costs a lot upfront, but that makes later changes, generalizations and refactorings cheaper and safer than they are with traditional proofs.
